items.prompt: L1's 'Archive' button is correctly wired — the click handler fires, the request succeeds, the row disappears. Six of ten test users still never click it. What does this tell you?
choices: The click handler must actually be broken, despite what the code shows
Working code and a usable interface are different things — an element can be functionally correct and still fail to signal that it can be interacted with at all
The users simply weren't paying attention during the test
This only happens with slow network requests
items.explanation: Correct wiring means the code does what it was told when triggered. It says nothing about whether the element visibly invites being triggered in the first place — that's a separate property, and the plain-text button had zero signal of it.
items.reference:
Correct code

Handler fires, request succeeds

Usable interface

Looks like something you can click

Why: a bug-free handler can't compensate for an element that never looked interactive.

items.prompt: Per L1, why isn't 'the click handler works' a sufficient bar for calling an interaction done?
choices: It is sufficient — visual styling is a separate, optional concern
Because whether the click handler runs when triggered says nothing about whether a person will ever discover there's something to trigger
Because click handlers are always unreliable on mobile devices
It's only insufficient for destructive actions like delete
items.explanation: The handler answers 'what happens once clicked.' It has no bearing on the separate question of whether anyone notices the element is clickable to begin with — that gap is exactly what stranded six of ten test users.
items.reference:
Correct code

Handler fires, request succeeds

Usable interface

Looks like something you can click

Why: a bug-free handler can't compensate for an element that never looked interactive.

items.prompt: Per L1's door example, what's the actual distinction between an affordance and a signifier?
choices: They're the same thing described with two different words
The affordance is what the object can actually do (the door can be pulled); the signifier is the visible cue that communicates it (a 'pull' label)
A signifier is only relevant to physical objects, never software
An affordance is always a bug; a signifier is always the fix
items.explanation: The flat door plate never lacked the ability to be pulled — that affordance was always there. What it lacked was a signifier: something visible telling people which way to push or pull, without changing what the door itself can do.
items.reference:
🚪 Affordance: the door can be pulled (always true)
🏷️ Signifier: a 'pull' label (tells you so)

Why: a signifier can be added without changing what the thing underneath can actually do.

items.prompt: A flat metal door plate has no label. Per L1, does that door lack an affordance, a signifier, or both?
choices: It lacks the affordance entirely — the door genuinely cannot be pulled
It lacks only a signifier — the door can still be pulled, it just has nothing visible saying so
It lacks neither — flat plates are a signifier for pushing
The distinction doesn't apply to physical objects, only screens
items.explanation: The affordance (pullable) was never missing. What's missing is a signifier — a visible cue letting someone know which way the door opens before they try both.
items.reference:
🚪 Affordance: the door can be pulled (always true)
🏷️ Signifier: a 'pull' label (tells you so)

Why: a signifier can be added without changing what the thing underneath can actually do.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, three of the four users who did click 'Archive' clicked it two or three times each. What does that repeated clicking most directly indicate?
choices: The users didn't understand what 'archive' means
A missing feedback loop — nothing visibly confirmed the first click had registered, so they couldn't tell if it had worked
The button was actually broken and needed multiple clicks to function
The users were testing the button's durability on purpose
items.explanation: A feedback loop is what confirms an action landed. With no visible change for ~400ms, a user has no way to distinguish 'it worked and is just slow' from 'nothing happened' — so they click again to be sure, exactly as observed.
items.reference:
🔁 No confirmation → re-click to check
✅ Immediate confirmation → no need to re-click

Why: a feedback loop is what lets a user trust that one click was enough.

items.prompt: What is a 'feedback loop,' as L1 defines it?
choices: A decorative animation added purely for visual polish
The confirmation, after an action, that tells the user the action actually landed and what changed as a result
A loop in the underlying code that retries a failed request automatically
A synonym for a usability heuristic
items.explanation: A feedback loop is specifically about closing the gap between 'I did something' and 'I know what happened as a result' — without it, a user is left guessing whether their input registered at all.
items.reference:
🔁 No confirmation → re-click to check
✅ Immediate confirmation → no need to re-click

Why: a feedback loop is what lets a user trust that one click was enough.

items.prompt: Per L1, what's the actual value of using an established interaction pattern (a dropdown, a toggle, a modal) instead of inventing a custom one?
choices: Patterns are required by law in consumer software
The user's prior experience with that pattern elsewhere does the explaining for you, instead of every screen having to teach its own rules from scratch
Patterns are always visually simpler to build than custom interactions
Patterns eliminate the need for any feedback loop at all
items.explanation: A pattern's real payoff is borrowed familiarity — someone who has used a toggle switch before already knows what flipping this one will do, without the interface needing to teach it fresh.
items.reference:
🆕 Novel pattern: user learns from scratch, on this screen
♻️ Known pattern: prior experience explains it for free

Why: reusing a recognized pattern outsources the teaching to experience the user already has.

items.prompt: What is an 'interaction pattern,' most precisely, per L1?
choices: A specific color palette applied consistently across a product
A reusable, already-learned solution to a recurring interaction problem, like a dropdown for choosing one option or a modal for an interruption needing a decision
A legal requirement for accessible software
Any interactive element, regardless of how novel or familiar it is
items.explanation: A pattern is defined by being reusable and already-learned — its value comes specifically from being recognized, not from being any interactive element whatsoever.
items.reference:
🆕 Novel pattern: user learns from scratch, on this screen
♻️ Known pattern: prior experience explains it for free

Why: reusing a recognized pattern outsources the teaching to experience the user already has.

items.prompt: Per L1, how can an interaction stay predictable (using a familiar pattern) without feeling generic or boring?
choices: It can't — predictable and interesting are mutually exclusive
Personality can live in the surface (color, motion, icon style, copy) while the underlying rules of the pattern — what happens on click, hover, drag — stay consistent with what users already expect
By replacing every familiar pattern with a novel one on each screen
By adding as much animation as possible, regardless of the pattern underneath
items.explanation: The distinction L1 draws is between the pattern's model (its rules and implied behavior) and its skin (visual and motion treatment). Keeping the model consistent preserves speed and safety; varying the skin is where a product's personality can live without cost.
items.reference:
🔒 Keep consistent: what happens when you click/hover/drag
🎨 Free to vary: color, motion, icon style, copy

Why: the model is what makes an interaction safe and fast; the skin is where personality can live.

items.prompt: A team worries that using a standard checkbox pattern will make their settings page feel 'too generic.' Per L1, what's a way to add personality without abandoning the pattern's recognizability?
choices: Replace the checkbox with an entirely custom, never-seen-before shape
Keep the checkbox's checked/unchecked behavior and shape recognizable, and express personality through color, motion, or micro-interaction on top of it
Remove all visual styling entirely, leaving plain text
There's no way to do this — generic patterns are always generic
items.explanation: The pattern's core promise (its shape and its implied binary behavior) is what makes it instantly usable. Personality added on top — a satisfying check animation, a distinct color — doesn't threaten that recognizability the way replacing the shape entirely would.
items.reference:
🔒 Keep consistent: what happens when you click/hover/drag
🎨 Free to vary: color, motion, icon style, copy

Why: the model is what makes an interaction safe and fast; the skin is where personality can live.

items.prompt: Per L1, what's the actual skill this unit is trying to build?
choices: Memorizing a fixed list of every interaction pattern that exists
Noticing the gap between what an element can do and what it visibly says it can do
Being able to write CSS from memory without looking anything up
Choosing the most visually novel interaction for every screen
items.explanation: The unit's throughline is that a correctly working interaction can still fail a real person if it never signals its own affordance or confirms its own outcome — the skill is catching that gap, not memorizing a pattern catalog.
items.reference:
❓ What can it do?
vs.
👁️ What does it visibly say it can do?

Why: the gap between the two is where 'works but nobody uses it' bugs live.

items.prompt: In L1's scenario, what's the single change most directly responsible for making the 'Archive' label readable as clickable?
choices: Making the label's font size larger
Restoring signifiers such as a cursor change, hover state, and visible affordance cues that the plain-text version stripped away
Renaming the button from 'Archive' to something else
Making the request faster on the backend
items.explanation: The click handler and request were never the problem. What needed restoring were the visible cues — signifiers — that tell someone an affordance exists before they try it.
items.reference:
👻 Plain text: no signifier
👆 Cursor/hover/border restored: signal present

Why: the underlying affordance never changed — only whether it was communicated did.

items.prompt: Someone argues 'affordances and signifiers are just a fancy way of saying visual styling.' What's the flaw in that claim, per L1?
choices: There's no flaw — it's an accurate simplification
Affordance describes what an element can actually do, which is independent of styling; signifier is the specific subset of visual cues whose job is announcing that capability, not styling in general
The flaw is that affordances only apply to buttons, never other elements
The flaw is that signifiers are never visual at all
items.explanation: Affordance isn't visual at all — it's a functional fact about what the element can do. Signifier is visual, but narrowly scoped to communicating that function, not styling in the general decorative sense (color choices unrelated to interactivity, for instance).
items.reference:
⚙️ Affordance: functional, not visual at all
🏷️ Signifier: visual, but scoped to announcing function

Why: conflating the two with generic 'styling' misses what each one actually does.

items.prompt: Per L2, what are the four moments of the interaction loop, in order?
choices: Design, Build, Test, Ship
Signal, Act, Respond, Confirm
Hover, Click, Load, Redirect
Discover, Learn, Trust, Repeat
items.explanation: L2's model breaks a single interaction into a before-half (Signal: can I do something here?) and an after-half (Act, Respond, Confirm: did it register, is it working, what changed) — four distinct questions, not one single click event.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Signal — can I do something here?
2️⃣ Act — did my input register?
3️⃣ Respond — is it working on it?
4️⃣ Confirm — what changed?

Why: a click isn't one event — it's a round-trip with a before and an after.

items.prompt: Which question does the 'Respond' moment in L2's four-moment model answer?
choices: Can I do something here?
Did my input register at all?
Is the system currently doing what I asked?
What actually changed as a result?
items.explanation: Respond sits between Act (did the input register) and Confirm (what changed) — it's specifically about signaling that work is underway, such as a spinner during a slower request, distinct from the other three moments.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Signal — can I do something here?
2️⃣ Act — did my input register?
3️⃣ Respond — is it working on it?
4️⃣ Confirm — what changed?

Why: a click isn't one event — it's a round-trip with a before and an after.

items.prompt: Per L2's Checkpoint, a 'Save' button has a working press animation and a spinner, but looks identical to body text until hovered. Is the interaction fully fixed?
choices: Yes — Act and Respond are both covered, which is the hard part
No — Signal is still missing, and on a touch device with no hover at all, that entire group of users gets no signal whatsoever
Yes, because spinners always compensate for missing hover states
No, because press animations are never a real fix for anything
items.explanation: Each of the four moments has to hold on its own. Fixing Act and Respond doesn't substitute for Signal — and touch devices, which have no hover state, are left with zero indication the element is interactive at all.
items.reference:
✅ Act, Respond: fixed
❌ Signal: still missing, worse on touch (no hover)

Why: fixing three of four moments doesn't compensate for the fourth being absent for an entire user group.

items.prompt: Why does a hover-only signifier fail a specific, identifiable group of users, per L2?
choices: It doesn't fail anyone — hover works the same everywhere
Touch-screen users never trigger a hover state at all, so any signifier that depends solely on hover leaves them with no signal before they touch the element
Hover states are deprecated in modern browsers
It only fails users with slow internet connections
items.explanation: Hover is a pointer-device-only interaction; there's no equivalent gesture on touch before contact. A signifier that relies exclusively on hover simply doesn't exist for that entire class of device.
items.reference:
✅ Act, Respond: fixed
❌ Signal: still missing, worse on touch (no hover)

Why: fixing three of four moments doesn't compensate for the fourth being absent for an entire user group.

items.prompt: Per L2's CSS example, restoring `cursor: pointer`, a `:hover` background change, an `:active` scale, and a `:focus-visible` outline to a button changes what about the underlying element?
choices: It changes what the button actually does — the click handler and request logic
Nothing about what the button does — only the signifiers announcing that it can be interacted with, and confirming when it has been
It changes the button's accessibility role entirely
It removes the need for the click handler
items.explanation: L2 is explicit: the click handler, the request, and the row removal are identical between the broken and fixed versions. Only the signals — Signal via cursor/hover, Act via active state, Signal-for-keyboard via focus-visible — changed.
items.reference:
cursor: pointerSignal (mouse)
:hoverSignal (mouse)
:activeAct
:focus-visibleSignal (keyboard)

Why: the underlying affordance never changed — only how it's communicated did.

items.prompt: Why does L2's fixed CSS example include `:focus-visible` specifically, in addition to `:hover`?
choices: `:focus-visible` is purely decorative and adds no functional coverage beyond `:hover`
Keyboard-only and screen-reader users never trigger `:hover` at all, so `:focus-visible` extends the same Signal to a group `:hover` alone leaves out entirely
`:focus-visible` is required only for legal compliance, not real usability
`:focus-visible` replaces the need for `:active` entirely
items.explanation: Hover requires a pointer device moving over the element — something a keyboard-only user never does. `:focus-visible` gives that same population an equivalent Signal when they tab to the element instead.
items.reference:
cursor: pointerSignal (mouse)
:hoverSignal (mouse)
:activeAct
:focus-visibleSignal (keyboard)

Why: the underlying affordance never changed — only how it's communicated did.

items.prompt: Per L2, what specifically does reusing a known interaction pattern (like a checkbox) buy you that a brand-new one can't?
choices: It's always faster to code than a custom interaction
The user's prior experience supplies the signifiers for free — a familiar shape already signals what it does without any custom teaching needed
Known patterns never need a feedback loop at all
Known patterns are the only ones that can be made accessible
items.explanation: L2's framing is specifically about signifiers being pre-supplied: a checkbox seen a thousand times before doesn't need explanation, because its shape alone already communicates 'binary choice' from prior experience.
items.reference:
🆕 Novel: every signifier discovered by trial
♻️ Known: prior experience supplies signifiers for free

Why: a pattern's value is borrowed familiarity, not aesthetics.

items.prompt: Per L2, why does using a toggle switch for a setting that actually requires a separate 'Save' button afterward count as a broken pattern, not just an unusual design choice?
choices: Because toggle switches are never appropriate for any setting
Because a toggle's recognized shape implies instant, reversible effect — pairing it with a delayed Save contradicts the promise the pattern itself makes
Because Save buttons are always a sign of a bug
Because toggles are only valid on mobile devices
items.explanation: The pattern was recognized correctly by the user, but it made an implicit promise (instant effect) that the actual behavior (needs a separate Save) doesn't keep — that mismatch is worse than an unfamiliar interaction, because it actively misleads someone who trusted the pattern.
items.reference:
🆕 Novel: every signifier discovered by trial
♻️ Known: prior experience supplies signifiers for free

Why: a pattern's value is borrowed familiarity, not aesthetics.

items.prompt: Per L2's quick check, a toggle switch flips to 'on' instantly, but the setting actually takes 3 seconds to apply on the server with no visible indication of that gap. Which moment is broken?
choices: Signal — the toggle gives no indication it's interactive
Confirm — the switch shows 'on' before the effect is real, which can lie if the server call later fails
Act — the toggle doesn't register the tap at all
None of the four moments — this is an acceptable design
items.explanation: The toggle visibly flips (Act is fine) but shows a completed state (Confirm) before the underlying change is actually real, meaning it can end up displaying something false if the delayed server call fails.
items.reference:
🔀 Toggle implies: instant effect
⏱️ Reality: 3-second delayed effect, unshown

Why: the toggle pattern's own implied promise makes a hidden delay worse than it would be behind a Save button.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say a hidden 3-second delay is worse behind a toggle switch than it would be behind a 'Save' button with the identical delay?
choices: It isn't worse — the delay is identical either way, so the pattern used doesn't matter
The toggle pattern itself implies instant effect, so the delay contradicts a promise the user just recognized and trusted; a Save button never made that promise in the first place
Toggle switches are always technically slower to render than buttons
Save buttons are incapable of having delays at all
items.explanation: This is the pattern's implied contract at work: recognizing a toggle comes with an expectation of immediacy baked in. A Save button carries no such expectation, so the same delay behind it is unremarkable rather than a broken promise.
items.reference:
🔀 Toggle implies: instant effect
⏱️ Reality: 3-second delayed effect, unshown

Why: the toggle pattern's own implied promise makes a hidden delay worse than it would be behind a Save button.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, which two signifiers both cover the 'Signal' moment for mouse/trackpad users specifically?
choices: `:active` style change and loading spinner
`cursor: pointer` and a `:hover` style change
`:focus-visible` ring and `:active` style change
Loading spinner and `:focus-visible` ring
items.explanation: L2's table lists both `cursor: pointer` and the `:hover` style change under Signal, both scoped to mouse/trackpad users specifically, distinct from `:focus-visible` which covers the same moment for keyboard users instead.
items.reference:
cursor: pointerSignal (mouse)
:hoverSignal (mouse)
:focus-visibleSignal (keyboard)

Why: different signifiers reach different user populations for the same moment.

items.prompt: A request takes 2 seconds to complete, and the interface shows nothing during that window — no spinner, no disabled button. Which moment does this leave unhandled?
choices: Signal
Act
Respond
Confirm
items.explanation: Respond is specifically the moment answering 'is the system currently doing what I asked' — a 2-second silent gap with no loading indicator leaves that question unanswered, distinct from Act (did the click register) or Confirm (what changed).
items.reference:
1️⃣ Signal — can I do something here?
2️⃣ Act — did my input register?
3️⃣ Respond — is it working on it?
4️⃣ Confirm — what changed?

Why: a silent wait with no in-progress indicator is specifically a missing Respond moment.

items.prompt: A file upload shows a progress bar while uploading, then a checkmark once it finishes. Which two moments does this pair of signals cover, respectively?
choices: Signal, then Act
Respond (the progress bar shows work in progress), then Confirm (the checkmark shows the outcome)
Act, then Signal
Confirm, then Respond, in that order
items.explanation: The progress bar answers 'is the system currently doing what I asked' — Respond. The checkmark afterward answers 'what actually happened' — Confirm. They're sequential and distinct, not interchangeable.
items.reference:
3️⃣ Respond — progress bar, work underway
4️⃣ Confirm — checkmark, outcome shown

Why: 'in progress' and 'done, here's the result' are two separate questions, answered at two separate moments.

items.prompt: An interface shows a spinner while a request is in flight, but once the request finishes, the spinner just disappears with no success or failure indication at all. Which moment is left unhandled?
choices: Signal
Act
Respond
Confirm
items.explanation: Respond was handled by the spinner (the user knows something is happening). Confirm — what actually happened as a result — is missing, since the spinner vanishing tells the user nothing about success or failure.
items.reference:
3️⃣ Respond — progress bar, work underway
4️⃣ Confirm — checkmark, outcome shown

Why: 'in progress' and 'done, here's the result' are two separate questions, answered at two separate moments.

items.prompt: In L3's task-app audit, only 12% of first-time users discovered the swipe-hold gesture on their own. Which single moment in the four-moment model is the actual bottleneck?
choices: Confirm — the green flash isn't satisfying enough
Signal — the row has no icon, handle, or hint of any kind, so nobody knows there's anything to try
Respond — the 400ms hold takes too long
Act — the swipe gesture itself is too hard to perform physically
items.explanation: L3's audit table shows the row communicates nothing at rest — no icon, handle, or hint. Since 88% never get past that starting point, the later moments (Act, Respond, Confirm) never even get exercised for most users.
items.reference:
SignalNothing on the row hints at interactivity
ActNo feedback during the hold
ConfirmArrives too late for most

Why: an earlier moment gates whether a later one is ever reached at all.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does fixing Signal matter more here than fixing Confirm, given that both moments have real gaps?
choices: It doesn't matter more — both should be fixed with equal priority regardless of order
Because 88% of users never get past Signal in the first place, so a better Confirm would only benefit the 12% who already succeeded
Because Confirm is technically impossible to fix on a mobile device
Because Signal is always the most important moment in every interaction, with no exceptions
items.explanation: L3's Checkpoint makes this explicit: fixing a later moment before an earlier one is solid only helps people who already got past the earlier gate. With Signal blocking 88% of users, that's where the fix has to start.
items.reference:
SignalNothing on the row hints at interactivity
ActNo feedback during the hold
ConfirmArrives too late for most

Why: an earlier moment gates whether a later one is ever reached at all.

items.prompt: The task-app team's first instinct is to make the green 'done' flash brighter and longer, hoping a better payoff will drive more people to find the gesture. Per L3's Checkpoint, is this the right first fix?
choices: Yes — a more satisfying reward always increases discovery
No — 88% of users never complete the gesture at all, so they never reach the flash; a louder Confirm only rewards the 12% who already succeeded
Yes, because Confirm is always the most impactful moment to improve
No, because green flashes are inherently a bad design choice
items.explanation: The usability numbers show the bottleneck is earlier in the loop. Improving the reward at the end doesn't help people who never reach the end — the fix has to address why people don't attempt or complete the gesture in the first place.
items.reference:
📉 88% never complete the gesture
✨ A louder flash only rewards the 12% who already did

Why: the ordering in the four-moment model isn't arbitrary — earlier moments gate later ones.

items.prompt: Per L3, what's the general lesson from the team's mistaken instinct to fix Confirm first?
choices: Confirm should never be improved under any circumstances
Diagnose which moment is the actual bottleneck before investing effort — improving a later moment doesn't compensate for an earlier one blocking most of the audience from ever reaching it
All four moments should always be fixed simultaneously, regardless of measured impact
Usability testing is unreliable and shouldn't guide these decisions
items.explanation: The broader point is diagnostic ordering: measure where users actually drop off, and fix that moment first. Intuition ('make the reward better') can point at the wrong moment if it isn't checked against where people are actually failing.
items.reference:
📉 88% never complete the gesture
✨ A louder flash only rewards the 12% who already did

Why: the ordering in the four-moment model isn't arbitrary — earlier moments gate later ones.

items.prompt: L3's actual fix adds a permanent visible circle to each row, tappable on its own, while keeping the swipe gesture available for anyone who already knows it. What does this design achieve?
choices: It removes the swipe gesture entirely, replacing it with only the circle
It gives first-time users a discoverable path (the visible circle) while preserving the swipe as a faster accelerator for people who've already learned it
It makes the swipe gesture mandatory for both new and experienced users
It has no effect on discoverability, only on visual appearance
items.explanation: The fix keeps both paths: a guessable, always-visible default for novices, and a faster shortcut underneath for people already fluent — the same 'novice path plus expert accelerator' idea used elsewhere in this track.
items.reference:
⭕ Visible circle: discoverable default (novice path)
👆 Swipe/hold: kept as a faster accelerator

Why: a visible fallback doesn't require removing the shortcut for people who've already learned it.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does the fix keep the swipe gesture in the product at all, instead of removing it once the visible circle is added?
choices: Because removing existing gestures always breaks backward compatibility technically
Because for people who've already learned the swipe, it's a genuinely faster accelerator, and there's no reason to force everyone onto the slower discoverable path once they no longer need it
Because the visible circle alone is not technically capable of triggering the 'done' action
Because usability testing showed the swipe gesture is preferred by 100% of users
items.explanation: The circle solves discoverability; the swipe remains valuable for speed once someone already knows it exists. Removing the swipe would trade away real efficiency for no discoverability gain, since the circle already covers that.
items.reference:
⭕ Visible circle: discoverable default (novice path)
👆 Swipe/hold: kept as a faster accelerator

Why: a visible fallback doesn't require removing the shortcut for people who've already learned it.

items.prompt: Per L3, under what condition is inventing a novel, less-discoverable interaction actually a defensible trade-off rather than a mistake?
choices: Whenever the design team personally prefers how it looks
When the audience will use the product often enough to learn it once and benefit from the speed repeatedly, or when the novelty is paired with an explicit, temporary teach like a coach mark
Whenever the interaction is technically simpler to implement
Never — novel interactions are always a mistake regardless of context
items.explanation: L3 names two specific conditions: high-frequency use where a one-time learning cost pays off repeatedly, or novelty paired with real, explicit teaching. Neither condition applied to the original hidden swipe gesture, which is why it was a mistake there specifically.
items.reference:
🔁 High-frequency use: learning cost pays off repeatedly
💡 Paired with explicit, temporary teaching

Why: novelty isn't wrong by default — it's wrong when neither condition holds and there's no visible fallback.

items.prompt: Per L3, what specifically made the original task-app swipe gesture the wrong call, given that novelty can sometimes be justified?
choices: Novelty is always wrong, with no exceptions, so this was inevitable
It was the only way in, for a casual consumer audience that includes many first-time users who won't use the app often enough to stumble into it — neither justifying condition applied
The gesture was technically broken and never actually functioned
Green was the wrong color choice for the confirmation flash
items.explanation: L3 is specific: the mistake wasn't inventing the gesture, it was making it the *only* path for an audience with many first-time, infrequent users — exactly the population neither justifying condition (frequent use, or an explicit teach) covers.
items.reference:
🔁 High-frequency use: learning cost pays off repeatedly
💡 Paired with explicit, temporary teaching

Why: novelty isn't wrong by default — it's wrong when neither condition holds and there's no visible fallback.

items.prompt: Per L3's Checkpoint, a team adds a one-time coach mark explaining the swipe gesture on first launch, but keeps the swipe as the only way to mark a task done, with no permanent visible fallback. Does this fully solve the discoverability problem?
choices: Yes, fully — a coach mark is equivalent to a permanent visible signifier
Not fully — someone who dismisses it quickly, gets interrupted, or forgets it later is back to a row with no ongoing signal at all
Yes, because coach marks are shown every single time the app opens
No, because coach marks are never useful for anything
items.explanation: A coach mark is a one-time, catchable moment; a permanent visible element is a durable, always-available fallback. The former can help but doesn't substitute for the latter, since it can be missed, forgotten, or dismissed without absorbing.
items.reference:
💬 Coach mark: one catchable moment
⭕ Permanent circle: always there to fall back on

Why: a one-time teach is a reasonable addition to a permanent signal, but a weak replacement for one.

items.prompt: Per L3, what's the practical difference between a coach mark and a permanent visible signifier, in terms of what each one actually guarantees?
choices: There's no practical difference — both guarantee the same thing
A coach mark guarantees a signal only at one moment, dependent on the user catching and retaining it; a permanent element guarantees the signal is available every time the user looks, indefinitely
A coach mark is a stronger guarantee because it appears with an animation
A permanent signifier is weaker because it can be visually ignored just as easily
items.explanation: The coach mark's guarantee depends entirely on the user's attention and memory at one specific moment; a permanent signifier doesn't depend on either, since it's simply there every time the row is looked at, with no memory required.
items.reference:
💬 Coach mark: one catchable moment
⭕ Permanent circle: always there to fall back on

Why: a one-time teach is a reasonable addition to a permanent signal, but a weak replacement for one.

items.prompt: L3's third fix makes the row tilt and dim proportionally during the swipe-hold, instead of staying static until the full 400ms completes, and visibly resets if released early. Which moment does this specifically improve?
choices: Signal — it makes the row look interactive at rest
Act — it confirms the input is being noticed even mid-gesture, and admits when an attempt doesn't finish
